items.question: Why do you think Nvidia should build a computing platform for humanoid robots and intelligent robots in general?
items.object: Nvidia’s computing platform for intelligent robots
items.answer: So from the chip level, which is the J and Thor family, to the foundation model, Project Groot, and also to the simulation and the utilities that we build along the way, it will become a platform, a computing platform for humanoid robots and intelligent robots in general. I want to quote Jensen here. One of my favorite quotes from him is that everything that moves will eventually be autonomous, and I believe in that as well. It's not right now, but let's say 10 years or more from now. If we believe that there will be as many intelligent robots as iPhones, then we'd better start building that.

items.question: Why did you see World of Bits, the project to control computers from screen pixels, as an approach to AGI?
items.object: World of Bits and its computer-control interface
items.answer: During my time at OpenAI, we were already talking about AGI back in 2016. Back then my intern mentors were Andrej Karpathy and Ilya Sutskever, and we talked about and discussed a project together. It's called World of Bits. The idea is very simple: we want to build an AI agent that can read computer screens, read the pixels from the screens, and then control the keyboard and mouse. If you think about it, this interface is as general as it can get. All the things that we do on a computer, like replying to emails, playing games, or browsing the web, can all be done in this interface, mapping pixels to keyboard and mouse control. That was my first attempt at AGI at OpenAI, and also my first journey, the first chapter of my journey in AI agents.

items.question: How do you assess the limitations of reinforcement learning for the computer-control agents you worked on in 2016?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for computer-control agents in 2016
items.answer: Back then, the main method that we used was reinforcement learning. There was no transformer back in 2016. The thing is, reinforcement learning works on specific tasks, but it doesn't generalize. We can't give the agent arbitrary language and instruct it to do arbitrary things that we can do with a keyboard and mouse. Back then, it kind of worked on the task that we designed, but it doesn't really generalize.

items.question: How do you understand the Stanford Vision Lab's transition from static computer vision to embodied computer vision during your PhD?
items.object: The Stanford Vision Lab's transition to embodied computer vision
items.answer: During my time at Stanford, from 2016 to 2021, I witnessed the transition of the Stanford Vision Lab, led by Fei-Fei, from static computer vision, like recognizing images and videos, to more embodied computer vision, where an agent learns perception and takes actions in an interactive environment. This environment can be virtual, as in simulation, or it can be the physical world. That was my PhD, transitioning to embodied AI.

items.question: How do you conceptualize the mission of NVIDIA's Generalist Embodied Agent Research team across virtual and physical worlds?
items.object: NVIDIA's Generalist Embodied Agent Research (GEAR) team
items.answer: The team that I am co-leading right now is called GEAR, which stands for Generalist Embodied Agent Research. To summarize what our team works on in three words: we generate actions. We build embodied AI agents, and those agents take actions in different worlds. If the actions are taken in the virtual world, that would be gaming AI and simulation. If the actions are taken in the physical world, that will be robotics. Earlier this year in March, at GTC, Jensen's keynote unveiled something called Project Groot, NVIDIA's moonshot effort at building foundation models for humanoid robotics. That's basically what the GEAR team is focusing on right now. We want to build the AI brain for humanoid robots and even beyond.

items.question: What do you see as NVIDIA’s competitive advantages in building foundation models for robotics?
items.object: NVIDIA’s competitive advantages in building foundation models for robotics
items.answer: One is, for sure, compute. All of these foundation models require a lot of compute to scale up, and we do believe in scaling laws. There were scaling laws for LLMs, but the scaling laws for embodied AI and robotics are yet to be studied, so we're working on that. The second strength of NVIDIA is simulation. Before NVIDIA was an AI company, it was a graphics company. NVIDIA has many years of expertise in building simulation, like physics simulation and rendering, and real-time acceleration on GPUs. We are using simulation heavily in our approach to build robotics.

items.question: How do you think internet data, simulation data, and real robot data should fit together in a successful robotics strategy?
items.object: GEAR’s robotics data strategy
items.answer: We need all kinds of data, and simulation and real-world data by themselves are not enough. At GEAR, we divide this data strategy into roughly three buckets. One is internet-scale data, like all the text and videos online. The second is simulation data, where we use NVIDIA simulation tools to generate lots of synthetic data. The third is real robot data, where we collect the data by teleoperating the robot and recording those data on the robot platforms. I believe a successful robotic strategy will involve the effective use of all three kinds of data, mixing them, and delivering a unified solution.

items.question: How do you see the strengths and limitations of internet data for training a robot foundation model?
items.object: Internet data for robot foundation models
items.answer: Internet data are the most diverse. They encode a lot of common-sense prior. Most of the videos online are human-centered because humans love to take selfies and record each other doing all kinds of activities. There are also a lot of instructional videos online, so we can use that to learn how humans interact with objects and how objects behave under different situations. That provides a common-sense prior for the robot foundation model. But internet-scale data don't come with actions. We cannot download the motor control signals of robots from the internet.

items.question: What do you see as the strength of using simulation to generate robotics training data?
items.object: Simulation as a source of robotics training data
items.answer: In simulation, you can have all the actions and observe the consequences of the actions in that particular environment. The strength of simulation is that it's basically infinite data, and the data scales with compute. The more GPUs you put into the simulation pipeline, the more data you will get. The data is super real-time. If you collect data only on the real robot, then you are limited by 24 hours per day. But in simulation, with GPU-accelerated simulators, we can accelerate real time by 10,000x, so we can collect data at much higher throughput given the same clock time.

items.question: What do you see as the weaknesses of simulation data for robotics?
items.object: Simulation data for robotics
items.answer: The weakness I see is that, no matter how good the graphics pipeline is, there will always be this simulation-to-reality gap. The physics will be different from the real world, and the visuals will still be different; they will not look exactly as realistic as the real world. There is also a diversity issue: the contents in the simulation will not be as diverse as all the scenarios that we encounter in the real world.

items.question: How do you see the role of real robot data in a successful robotics data strategy?
items.object: Real robot data within a combined robotics data strategy
items.answer: Going to real robot data, those data don't have the sim-to-real gap because they're collected on the real robot, but they're much more expensive to collect because you need to hire people to operate the robots. Again, they're limited by the speed of the world of atoms: you only have 24 hours per day, and you need humans to collect those data, which is also very expensive. We see these three types of data as having complementary strengths. I think a successful strategy is to combine their strengths and remove their weaknesses.

items.question: How do you see the timeline from a research breakthrough in robot foundation models to robots entering people's daily lives?
items.object: A GPT-3 moment for robotics and the path to mass-market robots
items.answer: This is pure speculation, but I hope that we can see a research breakthrough in robot foundation models, maybe in the next two to three years. That's what we call a GPT-3 moment for robotics. After that, it's a bit uncertain. To have robots enter the daily lives of people, there are a lot more things than just the technical side. The robots need to be affordable and mass-produced, and we also need safety for the hardware, privacy, and regulations. Those will take longer for the robots to be able to hit a mass market, so that's a bit harder to predict. But I do hope that the research breakthrough will come in the next two to three years.

items.question: How do you think about robotics through the system one and system two framework from Thinking, Fast and Slow?
items.object: The system one and system two framework for robotics
items.answer: I would like to think about robotics as consisting of two systems: system one and system two. That comes from the book Thinking, Fast and Slow, where system one means low-level motor control that's unconscious and fast. For example, when I'm grasping this cup of water, I don't really think about how I move the fingertip at every millisecond. That would be system one. System two is slow and deliberate, more like reasoning and planning that uses the conscious brain power that we have.

items.question: What would you consider a GPT-3 moment for robotics?
items.object: A GPT-3 moment for robotics
items.answer: I think the GPT-3 moment will be on the system one side. My favorite example is the verb “open.” Just think about the complexity of the word “open.” Opening the door is different from opening a window, a bottle, or your phone. But humans have no trouble understanding that “open” means different things when you're interacting with different objects; it means different motions. So far, we have not seen a robotics model that can generalize on a low-level motor control on these verbs. I hope to see a model that can understand these verbs in their abstract sense and generalize to all kinds of scenarios that make sense to humans. We haven't seen that yet, but I'm hopeful that this moment could come in the next two to three years.

items.question: How do you see the challenge of integrating system two reasoning with system one in a robot foundation model?
items.object: Integrating system two reasoning with system one in robot foundation models
items.answer: For system two, we have already seen very strong models that can do reasoning and planning, and also coding. These are the LLM and frontier models that we have already seen these days. But integrating the system two models with system one is another research challenge in itself. The question is, for a robot foundation model, do we have a single monolithic model, or do we have some kind of cascaded approach where the system two and the system one models are separate and can communicate with each other in some ways? I think that's an open question.

items.question: How do you assess the tradeoffs of using a single monolithic robot foundation model for system two reasoning and system one motor control?
items.object: A monolithic robot foundation model combining system two and system one
items.answer: I see pros and cons. The monolithic model is cleaner; there's just one model, one API to maintain. But it's a bit harder to control because you have different control frequencies. The system two models will operate on a slower control frequency, let's say one hertz, one decision per second.

items.question: Why are you optimistic that scaling transformers can lead to breakthroughs in embodied AI?
items.object: Transformers and scaling laws for embodied AI
items.answer: I certainly hope that the data strategy I described will get us there, because I feel that we have not pushed the limit of transformers yet. On the essential level, transformers take tokens in and output tokens, and ultimately the quality of the tokens determines the quality of the model, the quality of those large transformers. For robotics, as I mentioned, the data strategy is very complex. We have all the internet data, and also need simulation data and real robot data. Once we're able to scale up on the data pipeline with all those high-quality actions, then we can tokenize them and send them to a transformer to compress. I feel we have not pushed transformers to the limit yet. Once we figure out the data strategy, we may be able to see some emerging property as we scale up the data and the model size. For that, I'm calling it the scaling law for embodied AI, and it's just getting started. I'm very optimistic that we will get there.

items.question: Why do you see humanoid robots as a compelling main research focus?
items.object: Humanoid robots as a main research focus
items.answer: There are a few reasons that we chose humanoid robots as the main research case to tackle. One reason is the world is built around the human embodiment, the human form factor. All our restaurants, factories, hospitals, equipment, and tools are designed for the human form and the human hands. In principle, a sufficiently good humanoid hardware should be able to support any task that a reasonable human can do. The humanoid hardware is not there yet today, but I feel in the next two to three years the humanoid hardware ecosystem will mature, and we will have affordable humanoid hardware to work on. Then it will be a problem about the AI brain, about how we can drive those humanoid hardware.

items.question: Why do you see humanoid robots as a practical starting point for training models that could eventually control other robot forms?
items.object: Humanoid robots as a starting point for training robot models
items.answer: There are also a bit more practical reasons in terms of the training pipeline. There is lots of data online about humans. It's all human-centered: all the videos of humans doing daily tasks, all having fun. The humanoid robot form factor is closest to the human form factor, which means that the model that we train using all of those data will have an easier time transferring to the humanoid form factor rather than the other form factors. For robot arms, how many videos do we see online about robot arms and grippers? Very few. But there are many videos of people using their five-finger hands to work with objects. It might be easier to train for humanoid robots, and then once we have that, we'll be able to specialize them to robot arms and more specific robot forms.

items.question: Why do you favor a generalist approach to AI over building separate models for specialized tasks?
items.object: The generalist approach to AI and specialized generalists
items.answer: I would like to first talk about the success story in NLP that we have all seen. Before ChatGPT and GPT-3, in the world of NLP there were a lot of different models and pipelines for different applications, like translation, coding, doing math, and creative writing. They all used very different models and completely different training pipelines. But then ChatGPT came and unified everything into a single model. Before ChatGPT, we called those specialists, and then GPT-3 and ChatGPT we call the generalists. Once we have the generalists, we can prompt them, distill them, and fine-tune them back to the specialized tasks, and we call those the specialized generalists. According to the historical trend, it's almost always the case that the specialized generalists are far stronger than the original specialists. They're also much easier to maintain because you have a single API that takes text in and spits text out.
quotes: I would like to first talk about the success story in NLP that we have all seen. items.answer: I think we can follow the same success story from the world of NLP, and it will be the same for robotics. Right now in 2024, most of the robotics applications we have seen are still in the specialist stage. They have specific robot hardware for specific tasks, collecting specific data using specific pipelines. Project Groot aims to build this general-purpose foundation model that works on humanoid first but later will generalize to all kinds of different robot forms or embodiments. items.answer: The idea is we will have the full stack as a unified solution to the customers. items.question: What makes Eureka a research project you're particularly happy about?
items.object: Eureka, a project using an LLM to write robot reward functions
items.answer: One work that I was really happy about was called Eureka. For this work, we did a demo where we trained a five-finger robot hand to do pen spinning. Very useful, and it's superhuman with respect to myself, because I have given up pen spinning long since childhood. I'm not able to do it live. I will fail miserably at this live demo. The robot hand is able to. The idea that we use to train this is that we prompt an LLM to write code in the simulator API that NVIDIA has built. It's called the Isaac Sim API. The LLM outputs the code for a reward function. A reward function is basically a specification of the desirable behavior that we want the robot to do. The robot will be rewarded if it's on the right track or penalized if it's doing something wrong.

items.question: Why do you see Eureka’s use of an LLM to design robot reward functions as a promising general-purpose technique?
items.object: Eureka’s approach to automating robot reward function design
items.answer: Typically, the reward function is engineered by a human expert, typically a roboticist who really knows about the API. It takes a lot of specialized knowledge, and reward function engineering is a tedious and manual task. What Eureka did was design an algorithm that uses an LLM to automate this reward function design, so the reward function can instruct the robot to do very complex things like pen spinning. It's a general-purpose technique that we developed, and we plan to scale this up beyond just pen spinning. It should be able to design reward functions for all kinds of tasks, or even generate new tasks using the NVIDIA simulation API. That gives us a lot of space to grow.

items.question: Why do you see falling humanoid robot prices as a reason for optimism about robotics now?
items.object: Humanoid robot pricing and manufacturing costs
items.answer: The second factor is pricing. We also see a significant drop in the price and manufacturing cost for humanoid robots. Back in 2001, NASA had a humanoid developed, and it's called a Robotnaut. I remember, if I recall correctly, it cost north of $1.5 million per robot. Most recently, there are companies that are able to put a price tag of about $30,000 on a full-fledged humanoid, and that's roughly comparable to the price of a car. There's always this trend in manufacturing where a mature product's price will tend towards the price of the raw material cost. For the humanoids, it typically takes only 4% of the raw material of a car. It's possible that we can see the cost trending downwards even more, and there could be an exponential decrease in the price in the next couple of years. That makes this state-of-the-art hardware more and more affordable.

items.question: Why do advances in foundation models make you optimistic about developing robot foundation models?
items.object: Foundation models for robotics
items.answer: We're able to see the system two problem, the reasoning and planning part, being addressed very well by the frontier models, like the GPTs and the Claudes and the Llamas of the world. These LLMs are able to generalize to new scenarios and write code. The Eureka project I just mentioned leverages these coding abilities of the LLM to help develop new robot solutions. There is also a surge in multimodal models improving computer vision and perception. I think these successes encourage us to pursue robot foundation models because we think we can ride on the generalizability of these frontier models and add actions on top of them, so we can generate action tokens that will ultimately drive these humanoid robots.

items.question: What was your thinking behind using code as the way for the Voyager agent to act in Minecraft?
items.object: Voyager’s use of code as actions in Minecraft
items.answer: We had the idea of Voyager after GPT-4 came along because at that time it was the best coding model out there. We thought, hey, what if we use coding as action? We use an API to first convert the 3D Minecraft world into a text representation and then have the agent write code using the action APIs.

items.question: How do you think about the way Voyager learns reusable skills while interacting with Minecraft?
items.object: Voyager’s self-reflection loop and skill library
items.answer: Just like human developers, the agent is not always able to write code correctly on the first try. We give it a self-reflection loop where it tries something out, and if it runs into an error or makes some mistakes in the Minecraft world, it gets feedback and can correct its program. Once it's written the correct program, that's what we call a skill. We'll have it saved to a skill library so that in the future, if the agent faces a similar situation, it doesn't have to go through that trial-and-error loop again; it can retrieve the skill from the skill library. You can think of that skill library as a code base that the LLM interactively authored all by itself. There's no human intervention. The whole code base is developed by Voyager.

items.answer: We call it an automated curriculum. items.question: How do you see the relationship between embodied agents in video games and embodied agents in robotics?
items.object: Shared principles between gaming agents and robotics
items.answer: As different as gaming and robotics seem to be, I see a lot of similar principles shared across these two domains. Embodied agents take perception as input, which can be a video stream along with some sensory input, and then they output actions. In the case of gaming it will be keyboard and mouse actions, and for robotics it will be low-level motor controls. Ultimately, the API looks like this. These agents need to explore in the world. They have to collect their own data in some ways. That's what we call reinforcement learning and self-exploration, and that principle is again shared among the physical agents and the virtual agents.

items.question: Why do you see robotics as harder than gaming for training embodied agents?

items.answer: I see robotics as harder because you also have a simulation-to-reality gap to bridge. In simulation, the physics and the rendering will never be perfect, so it's really hard to transfer what you're learning in simulation to the real world. That is by itself an open-ended research problem. Robotics has the sim-to-real issue, but gaming doesn't; you are training and testing in the same environment.

items.question: How do you envision a Foundation Agent generalizing across virtual and physical agents?
items.object: Foundation Agent
items.answer: Last year I proposed a concept called Foundation Agent, where I believe ultimately we will have one model that can work on both virtual agents and physical agents. For the foundation agent, there are three axes over which it will generalize: number one is the skills that it can do; number two is the embodiments, or the body form, the form factor it can control; and number three is the world, the realities it can master. In the future, I think a single model will be able to do a lot of different skills on a lot of different robot forms or agent forms, and then generalize across many different worlds, virtual or real. That's the ultimate vision that the GEAR team wants to pursue.

items.answer: I just think the virtual world and the physical world ultimately will just be different realities on a single axis. Let me give one example. There is a technique called domain randomization. How it works is that you train a robot in simulation, but you train it in 10,000 different simulations in parallel. For each simulation, they have slightly different physical parameters: the gravity is different, the friction, the weight, everything is a bit different. It's actually 10,000 different worlds.

items.object: Generalization from simulation to the physical world
items.answer: Let's assume we have an agent that can master all the 10,000 different configurations of reality all at once. Then our real physical world is just the 10,001st virtual simulation. In this way we're able to generalize from sim to real directly. That's exactly what we did in a follow-up work to Eureka, where we're able to train agents using all kinds of different randomizations in the simulation and then transfer zero-shot to the real world without further fine-tuning.

items.question: How do you see the Dr. Eureka work pointing toward agents that can generalize to the real world?
items.object: Dr. Eureka and generalization from virtual worlds to the real world
items.answer: I do believe in the Dr. Eureka work, and I believe that if we have all kinds of different virtual worlds, including games, and if we have a single agent that can master all kinds of skills in all the worlds, then the real world just becomes part of this bigger distribution.

items.question: How do you use an LLM as a robot developer in Dr. Eureka to help robots generalize from simulation to the real world?
items.object: Dr. Eureka’s use of an LLM as a robot developer
items.answer: For the Dr. Eureka work, we built upon Eureka and still use an LLM as kind of a robot developer. The LLM is writing code, and the code is to specify the simulation parameters, like the randomization parameters. After a few iterations, the policy that we train in simulation will be able to generalize to the real world. One specific demo that we showed is that we can have a robot dog walk on a yoga ball, and it's able to stay balanced and even walk forward.

items.question: How do you assess whether transformer architectures have reached their limits for robot foundation models?
items.object: Transformer architectures for robot foundation models
items.answer: For robot foundation models, we haven't pushed the limit of the architecture yet. The data is a hard problem right now and it's the bottleneck because, as I mentioned earlier, we can't download those action data from the internet. They don't come with those motor control data. We have to collect it either in simulation or on the real robots. Once we have that, once we have a very mature data pipeline, then we'll just push the tokens to the transformers and have them compress those tokens, just like transformers predicting the next word on Wikipedia. We're still testing these hypotheses, but I don't think we have pushed the transformers to their limit yet.

items.question: How do you view alternative architectures to transformers, such as Mamba and test-time training?
items.object: Alternative architectures to transformers
items.answer: There is also a lot of research going on right now on alternative architectures to transformers. I'm super interested in those personally, like there are Mamba and recently there was test-time training. There are a few alternatives, and some of them have very promising ideas. They haven't scaled really to the frontier model performance, but I'm looking forward to seeing alternatives to transformers.

items.question: Why do you see promise in Mamba and test-time training models as alternatives to transformers?
items.object: Mamba and test-time training models
items.answer: I mentioned the Mamba work and also test-time training. These models are more efficient at inference time, so instead of transformers attending to all the past tokens, these models have inherently more efficient mechanisms. I see them holding a lot of promise, but we need to scale them up to the size of the frontier models and really see how they compare head-on with the transformer.

items.question: Why are you excited about AI video generation?

items.question: Why are you excited about coding models over the next 10 years?
items.object: Coding models and the long-term potential of coding agents
items.answer: I'm super excited about models that code. I think coding is such a fundamental reasoning task that also has huge economic value. Maybe 10 years from now we'll have coding agents that are as good as human-level software engineers, and then we'll be able to accelerate a lot of development using the LLMs themselves.

items.question: What do you hope humanoid robotics will achieve over the next ten years?
items.object: Humanoid robots over the next ten years
items.answer: I think 10 years from now we'll have humanoid robots that are at the reliability and agility of humans or even beyond, and I hope at that time Project Groot will be a success and we'll be able to have humanoids helping us in our daily lives. I just want robots to do my laundry.

items.question: How do you think your PhD advisor Fei-Fei shaped your research taste?
items.object: Fei-Fei's influence on Jim Fan's research taste and move into embodied AI
items.answer: I admire my PhD advisor, Fei-Fei. I think she taught me how to develop good research taste. Sometimes it's not about how to solve a problem, but identify what problems are worth solving. The “what” problem is much harder than the “how” problem. During my PhD years with Fei-Fei, I transitioned to embodied AI. In retrospect, this is the right direction to work on. I believe the future of AI agents will be embodied, for robotics or for the virtual world.

items.question: How would you advise AI founders to use recent research and open-source tools to find worthwhile problems to solve?
items.object: Recent AI research papers and open-source tools as resources for founders choosing problems to solve
items.answer: Recent research papers: I feel that the research papers these days are becoming more and more accessible, and they have some really good ideas. They're more and more practical instead of just theoretical machine learning. I would recommend keeping up with the latest literature and also just trying out all the open-source tools that people have built. For example, at NVIDIA we built simulator tools that everyone can have access to. Just download it and try that out, and you can train your own robots in the simulations. Just get your hands dirty.
